Benjamin Lee Whorf. The American linguist best known for developing the theory of linguistic relativity, which proposes that the structure of a speaker's language influences how they perceive reality and their worldview. He proposed the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, named for him and his mentor Edward Sapir, claiming that linguistic categories determine or heavily influence thought patterns and cultural behaviour. His analysis of the Hopi language became particularly influential. He argued that its radically different tense system, which lacks the past, present, and future distinctions found in English, reflects and shapes a non-linear perception of time. Beyond his theoretical work, Whorf had an unusual career for a prominent linguist. He worked as a fire inspector for an insurance company by day while conducting linguistic research and theory-building in the evenings. He made strong claims about how language structure constrains reality perception, arguing that different languages entail fundamentally different worldviews or cosmologies. His work has been both highly influential and controversial. Critics argue he overstated the extent to which language determines thought, though his research with Edward Sapir remains central to modern cognitive science.
